main.text: b) Pistacia.

In the region: P. Lentiscus L. [=Linnaeus], P. mutica Fisch. et Mey. [=Fischer et Meyer], P. Terebinthus L. and var. [=varietas] Palaestina Engl. [=Adolf Engler] (= P. Palaestina Boiss. [=Pierre Edmond Boissier]) P. [=George E. Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] rocky slopes near Brummana in Lebanon (Bornmüller [=Jos. Bornmüller, Ein Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Flora von Syrien und Palästina] 30), P. vera L. B. Zisik [=?] gives the following ph [=Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew (modern)] designations: P. Lentiscus L. שיח לוט (after B. r. [=Bereshit Rabba, ed. Theodor and Albeck] 91, 11). P. Palaestina Boiss. אֵלָה (arab. [=Arabic] buṭm); P. mutica Fisch. et Mey. בטמה; P. vera L. בטנה (arab. fistuḳ) (Hasade [=Hasade, Hebrew agricultural monthly] 6, 206).
1. Pistacia Terebinthus L. Terebinth; turpentine tree.

Terebinth, merges by imperceptible gradations into var. Palaestina Engl., who is more common in our district then type. Rocky places and hillsides (Post [=George E. Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] 206. Bornm. [=Jos. Bornmüller, Ein Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Flora von Syrien und Palästina] 30). The terebinth, buṭum, is the true tree of the highlands, under whose mighty crown one gladly rests in the shade (Musil [=Alois Musil, Arabia Petraea] 3, 15). The tree, incidentally, is not evergreen without exception (Fonck [=Leopold Fonck, Streifzüge durch die biblische Flora] 48). The terebinth is not very common in the mountains of Judah, but it is in the forest west of Nazareth and in the Carmel woodlands (ZDPV. [=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins] 8, 104. 108. 110). It is fairly widespread in southern and central Syria. [p. 192] A large tree northwest of Jerusalem: besides the unripe fruits, a quantity of beautiful outgrowths, like red corals, from the parasite Viscum cruciatum (13, 223).

Bh. [=Biblical Hebrew] ʾēlā,*) nom. unit. [=nomen unitatis] of ʾēlīm. So the ancient translators.**) There is no reason to doubt this evidently traditional explanation. Modern Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew also holds to this meaning (Hasade 1, 3, 32 — 4, 391).

Abulwalīd [=Abulwalīd Merwān ibn Ğanāḥ, Book of Hebrew Roots] follows the Targum: buṭmā, and gives for it Arabic buṭm. He is followed, as always, by Parḥōn [=Salomo ibn Parḥon, Maḥberet he-ʿArukh, ed. Stern]: buṭmā, a tall tree with edible fruits like myrtle berries. R. D. Kimḥī [=Rabbi David Kimḥī (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim / biblical commentaries] also cites the erroneous opinion that it means olmo, elm.

The terebinth is, next to the oak, the most imposing tree of Eretz Yisrael and was therefore an object of tree worship. Extraordinary age was ascribed to individual specimens: one near Hebron was said to be as old as the world (Jos. bj. [=Josephus, Bellum Judaicum] 4, 9, 7). In post-biblical times first in Sirach [=Ben Sira (Ecclesiasticus)] (24, 16): I spread out my branches like a terebinth.

The fruit is called bh. [=Biblical Hebrew] בטנה,***) pl. [=plural] בטנים. The word has erroneously been taken for pistachio†) (RDK. [=Rabbi David Kimhi, Sefer ha-Shorashim], Salomo Ibn Melech [=Salomo Ibn Melech, Mikhlal Yofi] u. a. [=and others]). Bochart [=Samuel Bochart, Hierozoicon] treated the question in detail. Wetzstein [=Johann Gottfried Wetzstein, notes communicated to Löw] (Pf. [=Immanuel Löw, Aramäische Pflanzennamen] 420) championed the error: “בטן is biblically pistachio; the Arabs and Jews transferred the name to the terebinth. The fruit of the terebinth is worthless in Eretz Yisrael. Only the poorest peasants grind it on the hand mill in order to have lamp oil for free. The fruit of the terebinth is not edible, because nobody will crack the pea-sized hard stone in order to get out the lentil-sized contents”.

Wetzstein is mistaken. The pea-sized berries, ḳḍāma, are gathered and eaten when they are red and ripe (Musil 3, 15). Edible oil, not only lamp oil, is made from them (ZDPV. 14, 4n. [=note]: bizr [p. 193] el-buṭm). The press residues are called in jüd. [=Jewish] aram. [=Aramaic] כוספא דבטמי (Hg. [=Halachot gedolot, ed. Hildesheimer] 58_{5. 29}).

Guigues [=P. Guigues, Le livre de l'art du Traitement de Najim Ad-Dyn Mahmoud] p. [=page] 39 says: The green grains, granum viride (الحبّة الخضراء [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ]) of the Middle Ages, are the fruits of the terebinth, P. Tereb. L. They have been confused with pistachios, fusṭuḳ, fruits of P. vera L. Nowadays, moreover, the green grains are still used as food. It is above all in Mesopotamia that the fruits of the terebinth, buṭm, are edible.

בטנה, bŏṭnā,*) [assyr. [=Assyrian] buṭnu, Zimmern AF. [=H. Zimmern, Akkadische Fremdwörter] 54; palmyr. [=Palmyrene] בר בוטן**) n. pr. [=nomen proprium] Chajes, Onomatolog. [=H. P. Chajes, Beiträge zur nordsemitischen Onomatologie] 12] also Mishnaic. Švi [=Mishnah tractate Shevi'it] 7, 5: בוטנא, LA. [=variant reading] בטנה (TŠvi [=Tosefta Shevi'it, ed. Zuckermandel] 5, 68_{14}, Schwarz [=A. Schwarz's Tosefta editions and commentary] p. 215), once also Targ. [=Targum] בוטנין Gn. [=Genesis] 43, 11.
boṭnā is a native tree, whereas pistachios are imported from abroad (j Dem. [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Demai] 2, 22^{b}_{69}). These come to Eretz Yisrael from northern Syria (Rosen [=?], Pf. 69).

In the cited Mishnah and T. [=Tosefta, ed. Zuckermandel] passage, young edible shoots, לולב, are spoken of. The following are named: a) זרדים, b) הרובים, c) אלה, d) בוטנה, e) אטדין, f) אדיל. c) according to Maimūnī [=Maimonides (commentary on the Mishnah)] correctly ballūṭ,***) d. h. [=that is] ʾallā oak, not ʾēlā! Gal. [=Galen, Opera omnia, ed. C. G. Kühn] 6, 644 βλαστοὶ τερμίνθου [blastoi terminthou]! e) ῥάμνου [rhamnou]. He says: the terebinth shoots are pickled in vinegar or brine (Sachau, Inedita [=Eduard Sachau, Inedita Syriaca] 95).

The place name bŏṭnā alone proves that the pistachio, foreign to the land, cannot be meant. As a place name Arabic buṭm occurs: Socin, Ortsapell. [=Albert Socin, article on Arabic place appellatives] ZDPV. 22, 18: challet il-buṭm terebinth valley 31, 199, maḳāṭiʿ el-buṭmi terebinth quarry (31, 183).

בטנה Jos. [=Joshua] 13, 26, according to Robinson [=Edward Robinson, Palästina] 3, 924, baṭne south of eṣ-ṣalt (Schwarz, Tebuot haareṣ [=Joseph Schwarz, Tevuot ha-Aretz] ed. [=edition] Luncz, p. 271 n [=note]). A place boṭnā also jAz. [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Avodah Zarah] 1, 39^{d}_{27} = בטנן B. r. 47 end. The fair at the terebinth ירידה של בוטנה (ZAW. [=Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft] 29, 217. 221). S. Klein [=Samuel Klein, professor in Jerusalem] has combined this with the market of בית האילם MT. 185_{17} Hoffm. [=Midrash Tannaim, ed. D. Hoffmann], בית אילנים Sifre 2, 306, 132_{6} Friedm. [=Sifre, ed. M. Friedmann].

With the place name bŏtnā Dérenbourg [=Joseph Derenbourg, probably Essai sur l'histoire et la géographie de la Palestine] has associated בטנית bŏṭnīt, a proselyte woman from boṭnā (Sabb. [=tractate Shabbat] 24, 5. Beza 3, 8. T. 3, 205_{27}. TMen [=Tosefta Menahot] 13, 533_{33}. [Pes. [=tractate Pesahim] 57^{a}] Ned. [=tractate Nedarim] 23^{a}. M. Zizit [=Massekhet Zizit] p. 23_{6} Kirchheim [=Raphael Kirchheim, Septem libri Talmudici parvi Hierosolymitani] = Semaḥ. [=tractate Semahot] 12 [p. 98_{12} Romm. [=Romm edition (Vilna) of the Talmud] קטנים read, with M. Zizit, Šibbŏlē [=Shibbole ha-Leket, ed. S. Buber] 341 Buber [=Salomon Buber] and R. [=Rabbi] Elia Wilna, בטנית. ZAW. 29, 216).

[p. 194] Aramaic buṭmā, from which arab. buṭm is borrowed, Fraenkel [=Siegmund Fraenkel, Die aramäischen Fremdwörter im Arabischen] 139. The single occurrence buṭnīm of the Targum is a learned conjecture. Talmudic buṭmā Rh. [=Rosh ha-Shanah] 23^{a}. Bb. [=Bava Batra] 80^{b}. jKil. [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Kilayim] 1, 27^{a}. Targ. Jes. [=Isaiah] 1, 30. 6, 13 (TW. [=Jacob Levy, Chaldäisches Wörterbuch über die Targumim] אלה). 1 S. [=1 Samuel] 17, 2. 2 S. [=2 Samuel] 18, 9. Hos. [=Hosea] 4, 13. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] and jGn. [=Jerusalem Targum on Genesis] 35, 4. The Samaritan has דחלתה (דהלאה), and thus misunderstood the word and thought of ʾelōᵃh.

bōṭem, which BJ. [=Eliezer Ben Jehuda, Millōn] cites from Aßafs [=Asaf Judaeus, medical book] boṭmīm, is not Hebrew: it has been retained from the Syriac original. Ph. [=Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew] Hasade 6, 206.

Syriac: ܒܛܡܬܐ [בטמתא] Bible translation for ʾēlā, ʾēlōn, ʾallā, ʾallōn, boṭnīm, lōṭ (rōtem). a) τερέβινθος [terebinthos], b) τέρμινθος [terminthos], c) κῶνος [kōnos]? — Neo-Syriac: bīṭmā, bīṭemtā, a terebinth-tree.

a) BB. [=Bar Bahlūl, Lexicon syriacum] 274. 790. 829_{18} (corrupted here). b) Gal.-Üb. [=Syriac translation of Galen] c) ? ܐܣܛܪܘܒܝܠܘܣ ܩܘܢܘܣ [אסטרובילוס קונוס] BB. 277_{10}. Arabic among the Syrians. d) بطم [buṭm] BB. 274. 277. e) الحبّة الخضراء [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ] BA. [=Bar ʿAlī, Syriac-Arabic lexicon] 2354. BB. 381 Honein [=Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq]. 829 corrupt. [=corrupted] ܩܘܠܘܦܘܢܝܣ [קולופוניס] 1796 (= kolophonia) *). 1934: الحبّة الخضراء الاكبر [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ al-akbar] ܦܪܘܛܡ ܒܛܡܬܐ [פרוטם בטמתא]. — Τερεβινθίνη (ῥητίνη) [Terebinthinē (rhētinē)] Gal.-Üb. 240. List [=Gottheil, A list of plants] 99. Sachau Inedita [=Sachau, Inedita Syriaca] 95. BB. 790. f) ܪܘܒܬܐ ܕܒܛܡܬܐ [רובתא דבטמתא] [Duval-Berth. [=Duval and Berthelot, La chimie au moyen âge II: L'alchimie syriaque] 2, 45]. BB. 801 corrupt. 790 = 180. g) القاوازا [al-qāwāzā] = h) علك النباط [ʿilk al-nabāṭ] **) [ἀλκυόνιον [alkyonion]? Is there perhaps a confusion of ܪܘܒܬܐ [רובתא] BB. 179 and ܕܘܒܬܐ [דובתא]?] Perhaps علك البطم [ʿilk al-buṭm]? Card. [=Cardahi, Al-lobab] j) φρυκτὴ ῥητίνη [phryktē rhētinē] ***) resina terebinthi PSm. [=Payne Smith, Thesaurus syriacus] 325 ܪܘܒܠܝܢ [רובלין]. Sergius [=Sergius of Rēšʿainā] calls f) ܢܛܡܬܐ [נטמתא] BB. 404. 546. 789 f. [=and the following (page)] 801. 1796.

The resin of the terebinth, buṭm, Musil [=Musil, Arabia Petraea III] 3, 230. Nuwairī [=an-Nuwairī, Nihāyat al-arab] (E. Wiedem. [=Wiedemann, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Naturwissenschaften] 49, 19). ^{1}) ʿilk el-buṭm, resin of the حبّة الخضراء [ḥabba khaḍrāʾ], comes from the Maghreb, Eretz Yisrael, Syria and neighboring regions. In distinction from it, pistachio resin is called ^{2}) ʿilk el-anbāṭ,†) while mastic is called ^{3}) ʿilk al-rūmī. Kašef [=Kachef er-rumūz, transl. Leclerc] Sha [=Steinschneider, Heilmittelnamen der Araber] 1393 ff. [=and the following (pages)] has ^{1}) and ^{3}) likewise, but ^{2}) without translation, and ^{4}) ʿilk šaǵar ul-fustuḳ: gum of the pistachio tree.

Arabic: buṭm (ZDPV. [=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins] 27, 25. 30, 134. Robinson [=Robinson, Palästina] 1, 346. 3, 221). Ascherson [=Ascherson, in Sitzungsberichte der Gesellschaft naturforschender Freunde zu Berlin 1882], Sitzungsberichte der naturforsch. [=naturforschender] Freunde 1882 21. II. Nr. [=number] 2, S. [=page] 13: beṭūm, in Algeria the Tripolitanian terebinth, probably P. atlantica Desf. [=Desfontaines]. It is a LW. [=loanword] (Fraenkel [=Fraenkel, Die aramäischen Fremdwörter im Arabischen] 139). The [p. 195] fruit of the buṭm tree: kḍāma (Musil 3, 152). Terebinth nuts, bizr el-buṭm, yield an edible oil (Mielck [=?] 16).

Jews: Bacher, Tanchum [=Bacher, Aus dem Wörterbuche Tanchum Jeruschalmi's] 43 for boṭnīm. Physicians: Sha 292. Berggren ms. [=Berggren manuscript of the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft]: boṭm = شجر الترمنتين [šajar al-turmantīn] Mowat, Alphita [=Mowat, Alphita: A Medico-Botanical Glossary] 5 albotm.

The Syrians have, besides boṭm, also الحبّة الخضراء [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ] (Sha 562) BA. 2354. BB. 274. 381. 829. Guigues [=Guigues, Le livre de l'art du Traitement de Najim Ad-Dyn Mahmoud] 39. Likewise Kroner, Maim. [=Kroner, edition of a medical treatise of Maimonides] passim, with the ital. [=Italian] translation זרע אטרבנטינא.
2. Pistacia Lentiscus L. [=Linnaeus] Mastic shrub.*)

A small evergreen tree or shrub. As a component of evergreen maquis it is certainly native throughout the whole Mediterranean region, from Syria and Eretz Yisrael to the Canary Islands, and also in North Africa (Hehn [=Hehn, Kulturpflanzen und Haustiere, 8th ed.] 429). Illustration in Vietz [=Vietz, Icones plantarum medico-oeconomico-technologicarum] 2, 11. In 1804 Vietz still praises the medicinal effects of mastic resin, whereas it is now official only in Austria (Strassburger ^{15} [=Strasburger et al., Lehrbuch der Botanik, 15th ed.] 577). Bloch [=Bloch, Sĕbīlē ʿōlam] 2, 82, probably the first among Jews, describes the tree and its resin. Modern Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew: האלה קשת העלים = سريس [sarīs] (Hasade [=Hasade, Hebrew agricultural monthly] 1, 3, 32). Inaccurately בטנים**) (3, 454. 4, 312), erroneously שיח הלוט (6, 206).

The tree also yields mastic (Haynald, Mézgák [=Haynald, A szentírási mézgák és gyanták termőnövényei] 14. 28) in Eretz Yisrael (P. [=Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] 207), but for commerce it has long been obtained (Benjamin v. [=of] Tudela, p. [=page] 20 of Grünhut's translation [=Grünhut, Die Reisebeschreibungen des R. Benjamin von Tudela]) only on the island of Chios, from a cultivated variety (Moeller ^{2} [=Moeller, Lehrbuch der Pharmakognosie, 2nd ed.] 431). The annual production averages 125,000 kg [=kilograms]. Josua Benveniste [=Joshua Benveniste, Śĕde Jĕhōšuaʿ], rabbi in Constantinople, reports in his commentary on jḤalla [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Ḥalla] 4, 9 f. 177^{d}, published in 1662, that in the Turkish Empire mastic might be produced only on the island of Chios (כיאו). Already Benjamin of Tudela can report about the island of Chios (כיא) only that 400 Jews live there and that the tree from which mastic מצטיקי is collected is found there (1, 25 Asher. [=Asher, The Itinerary of Rabbi Benjamin of Tudela]).

In the Middle Ages mastic was regarded as a remedy; today it is used for varnishes and putties. In the Orient it has been in use as a chewing resin since ancient times, and that of Eretz Yisrael was considered the best according to the testimony of Plinius [=Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia] (Killermann [=Killermann, Die Blumen des heiligen Landes] 1, 34). Plin. 14, 25 says: in oriente optimam tenuissimamque [resinam] terebinthi fundunt, dein lentisci, quam et masticen vocant. Naḥmani [=Nahmanides, Commentary on the Pentateuch] knows [p. 196] that an oil is obtained from mastic, as from other kinds of resin (صمغ [ṣamgh] צמגים) (Ki tissa [=?] 76^{b}).

Tournefort [=Tournefort, Relation d'un voyage du Levant] (st. [=died] 1708. Tschirch [=Tschirch, Handbuch der Pharmakognosie] 1, 906) reported on the production of mastic on the island of Chios (Scio).

Arabic مصطكى [maṣṭakā] is a loanword (Fraenkel 151), and it has also migrated further into Armenian (Hübschmann [=Hübschmann, Armenische Grammatik I: Armenische Etymologie] 248. ZDMG. [=Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft] 51, 304) and into the European languages.

For Arabic: E. Wiedem. 56, 340. mastik (P.) Vullers [=Vullers, Lexicon Persico-Latinum etymologicum] 2, 51 = رَمَاسى [ramāsā]. מצטכי Abulw. [=Abulwalīd Ibn Janāḥ, Kitāb al-uṣūl] 302 Bacher [=Bacher (ed.), Sepher haschoraschim of Abulwalîd]. Sha 1879, Syriac كيا [kayā] 1756. Physicians: Sha a. O. [=at the place cited] Kašef = كيا [kayā]. Abu Salt [=Abū ṣ-Ṣalt Umayya of Denia, treatise on simple drugs]: משטיגי. Estori ha-Farḥī [=Estori ha-Farḥi, Kaftor waferaḥ] writes מצטכא and, in the name of his father, identifies it with קטף (f [=folio] 421^{b} Ven. [=Venice edition 1549], 107^{b} Edelm. [=ed. Edelmann, Berlin 1852], p. 662 Luncz [=ed. Luncz, Jerusalem 1899]).
Mastic is adulterated with the resin of the ʾubhul (juniper): Ibn Bassām [=Ibn Bassām, Arabic author on market supervision] in E. Wiedem. 40, 177. 189.

Romance forms among Jews: משתיק (Abulw. 302 Bacher), מסתיקי, מסתיצי Mb. [=?] 31. 50. Menaḥem b. Salomo [=Menaḥem ben Salomo, author of Sechel tob] (1139) says: lōṭ is the resin of the tree שטינקי (lentisco). It is called in it. [=Italian]: משטיכו; it is a remedy and serves to strengthen the teeth (Sechel tob [=Menaḥem ben Salomo, Sechel tob, ed. Buber] p. 11.). — Grünbaum, Jüd.-span. Chrest. [=Grünbaum, Jüdisch-spanische Chrestomathie] 11 f.: almastig, almaciga משטיק (Semag [=Sefer Mitzwot Gadol of Moses of Coucy] lāwīn 65 f. 22^{a}). On account of the eulogies (blessings) appropriate to its fragrance, Tur [=Arbaʿa Ṭurim of Jacob ben Asher] and SchA [=Shulḥan ʿArukh] OCh. [=Oraḥ Ḥayyim] 216, 3 mention it — in the codices as מצטכי, in Zēdā lederech [=Ṣēdā la-derekh by Menaḥem ibn Zeraḥ] 64^{b} as מצתכין, מצטיכי, מסטיכי.

Since Luther [=Martin Luther, German translation of the Bible] had rendered צרי*) in Ez. [=Ezekiel] 27, 17 by mastic, this has been frequently repeated and is still retained by Rothstein [=Rothstein, translation of Ezekiel in Kautzsch (ed.), Die Heilige Schrift des Alten Testaments] in the Kautzsch Bible (on ^{c d e}) and by others. ṣŏrī is not mastic but storax (Flora [=Löw, Die Flora der Juden] 3, 390), as Raši [=Rashi] on ^{a}) quite correctly states. In accordance with our usage one translates balsam (Rothstein), just as Abulwalīd [=Abulwalīd Merwān ibn Ğanāḥ, Book of Hebrew Roots], paraphrasing, gives „tirjāḳ“, and as the Geonic explanation in Ibn Esra [=Abraham Ibn Ezra, commentary] understands by it a remedy compounded from 75 ingredients — that is, a theriac.

If Targ. j [=Targum Jerushalmi (Pseudo-Jonathan)] puts שרף (ו)קטף for it, it will mean storax. In any case Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] with שעיף, samar. [=Samaritan (Targum)] שעבה (LAA. [=variant readings] שעפה, שעבי, שאבה), means not mastic but probably storax, not „balsam“ in general. In Eretz Yisrael in Talmudic times (3rd—4th Jh. [=century]) [p. 197] people wrongly sought mastic in the lōṭ of the Bible, which confirms that ṣŏrī was not traditionally taken to be mastic (B. r. [=Bereshit Rabba, ed. Theodor and Albeck] 91, 11).

In Arabic P. Lent. is also called ضرو [ḍirw]. Nuwairī [=an-Nuwairī, Nihāyat al-arab] in E. Wiedem. [=Eilhard Wiedemann, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Naturwissenschaften] 49, 21 says that kamkām is the lentiscus resin of the tree ḍirw, according to others its leaves or bark. It flows out elastically, black as pitch. The tree resembles the terebinth, buṭm, according to others a very large oak, but is said to be smoother and more delicate. It bears clusters of fruit, like the buṭm. Used for toothpicks: Silberberg, Dināwarī [=Silberberg, Das Pflanzenbuch des Abū Ḥanīfa Aḥmed ibn Dāūd ad-Dīnawarī] 78.

The Midrash cited renders the bibl. [=biblical] lōṭ as mastic: מסטוכי (LA. [=variant reading] מסטכי, מסתיכי, corrupt. [=corrupted] מפטדי, correctly RDK. [=Rabbi David Kimhi, Sefer ha-Shorashim] sv. [=sub voce] lōṭ: מוצטכא) and adds: עבידא כול (LAA. [=variant readings] according to Albeck's [=Chanoch Albeck, co-editor of Bereshit Rabba, private communication]*) communication: עבידה בול, יעבידא כיל, עבירא כול, עביד הביל), which is probably meant to signify „in little lumps“. Menaḥem b. Salomo [=Menaḥem ben Salomo, author of Sechel tob] (1139) says: mustichi is like frankincense and consists of small grains like grains of salt.

In the tannaitic period mastic was chewed in Eretz Yisrael, either as a remedy or — as still today (Luncz zu Farḥi [=Estori ha-Farḥi, Kaftor wa-feraḥ, ed. Luncz, Luncz's notes] p. [=page] 662) — to improve the odor of the mouth — εὐωδία [euōdia] Diosk. [=Dioscorides, De materia medica] 1, 93 Spr. [=edition of Dioscorides by Sprengel] 1, 67 W. [=edition of Dioscorides by Wellmann] (Preuss [=Julius Preuss, Biblisch-talmudische Medizin] 195) TSabb. [=Tosefta Shabbat, ed. Zuckermandel] 12, 127_{8} מסטיכי (LA. מוסתכין, Maim. [=Maimonides] מסטכי, Codd. [=codices] מצטכי**) Maim. H. Sabb. [=Hilkhot Shabbat in Maimonides' Mishneh Torah] 21, 24)***). Tur [=Arbaʿa Ṭurim of Jacob ben Asher] SchA. [=Shulchan Arukh] OCh. [=Oraḥ Ḥayyim] 216, 3. 328, 36.: It may not be used as a remedy on the Sabbath, but it may be used as a cosmetic.

ZDMG. [=Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft] 28, 702 Rubber, Persian ḳenderan. Orientals like to produce a greater secretion of saliva by chewing resinous substances, such as mastic and pistachio resin (sakkis). Ḳenderan is used, a rubber-like mass made from the thickened latex of several species of Scorzonera and Podospermum.

[=Syriac] Diosk., calls the mastic tree the tree of the small black pistachios, which grows in Šārōn (read with Venetianer: Chios) and exudes mastic. It is called gr. [=Greek] chīnos, lat. [=Latin] lentiscus. Then follows the [p. 198] medicinal use according to Diosk. בוטנים לכל מיניהם designates in his work all species of Pistacia, for whose oils he gives the medicinal use according to Diosk. on p. 141.

[=Syriac translation of Galen] 281 List [=Gottheil, A list of plants]: μαστίχη [mastichē]: Aßaf מסטיכין = lentiscus = איסקינוס. Wine: ܥܣܘܪܐ ܕܒܛܡ ܐܝܠܢܐ ܕܒܛܡܐ [עסורא דבטם אילנא דבטמא]. PSm. [=R. Payne Smith, Thesaurus syriacus] 2179. 2239 f. [=and the following] ܡܫܚܐ ܕܒܛܡܘܬܐ [משחא דבטמותא] BB. 1167 دهن الضرو [duhn al-ḍirw] read ܕܒܛܡܐ [דבטמא].
3. Pistacia vera L. [=Linnaeus] True pistachio. Erroneously boṭnā Hasade [=Hasade, Hebrew agricultural monthly] 6, 206.

The true pistachio grows wild in Syria today (Hehn^{8} [=Victor Hehn, Kulturpflanzen und Haustiere, 8th ed.] 429). Ritter [=Carl Ritter, Erdkunde von Asien] 11, 561 has treated its Asiatic distribution in detail (Schrader RL. [=Otto Schrader, Reallexikon der indogermanischen Altertumskunde] 863).

Theophrast [=Theophrastus, Historia plantarum] (st. [=died] 280 v. C. [=before Christ]) describes a species of terebinth that occurs in Bactria, and means the true pistachio, whose name, however, he does not yet know. Only Nikander [=Nicander of Colophon, Theriaca], 150 B.C., names the pistachio, which grows by the Indian river Choaspes. The Syrian pistachios are first mentioned by Posidonius [=Posidonius of Apamea] (ca. 135—150 B.C.), from Apamea in Syria, as „so-called“ pistachios (βιστάκιον [bistakion]). Diosk., Plinius [=Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia] and Galen [=Galen, Opera, ed. Kühn] also know the Syrian pistachio nuts under the name pistakion. Galen already praises the pistachios of Aleppo (Beroea), where the tree is still widely cultivated today. Those originating from the pistachio grove near Herat (Ritter 8, 247) are more delicate and easier to open with the finger (17, 1727 f.). Besides Aleppo they are most frequent near Beirut, Tripoli, Baalbek and Damascus and in Rūm kalʿa on the Euphrates (ZDPV. [=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins] 11, 93). According to Edrīzī [=al-Idrīsī, Nuzhat al-muštāq], maʿarra exports many pistachios to all Syrian lands (Ritter 8, 138). On the present-day trade in Syria, Südenhorst, Syrien [=Südenhorst, Syrien und seine Bedeutung für den Welthandel] 28 reports. Added to this is the fact that the Mishnaic period, too, uses the borrowed name pistaḳin and designates the fruit as foreign. From this it follows that the boṭnīm of the patriarchal period do not mean pistachios. If the assyr. [=Assyrian] buṭnu (Zimmern, AF. [=H. Zimmern, Akkadische Fremdwörter] 54) is adduced for the meaning pistachio, this proves nothing, for according to Delitzsch HWB. [=Friedrich Delitzsch, Assyrisches Handwörterbuch] 171 this is a tree whose wood was used for building palaces; it will therefore probably mean another pistachio, perhaps the P. Khinjuk Stocks [=John Ellerton Stocks] of the Western Asiatic steppes or P. mutica Fisch. et Mey. [=Fischer et Meyer] of the eastern Mediterranean region from Asia Minor to Afghanistan (Hehn [=Victor Hehn, Kulturpflanzen und Haustiere] 429).

[p. 199] When Wetzstein [=Johann Gottfried Wetzstein, notes communicated to Löw] (Pf. [=Löw, Aramäische Pflanzennamen] 420) objects that the fruit of the terebinth is not edible, this is inaccurate, for Oken [=Lorenz Oken, Allgemeine Naturgeschichte für alle Stände] 1755 reports that the terebinth kernel is eaten in the Levant and therefore comes to market. The seeds are also eaten in Greece (see above 192).

Before the actual pistachio was introduced into Eretz Yisrael, the native terebinth kernel will have been more highly valued and could very well be mentioned among the export articles of antiquity. The Septuagint and the Vulgate therefore quite rightly understand boṭnīm as terebinth kernels.

Furrer [=Konrad Furrer, articles in Schenkel's Bibel-Lexikon] (Bibellexikon sv.) tries to get around the difficulty that the pistachio grows in Syria but not in Eretz Yisrael with the phrase that the pistachio is „nowadays“ rarely found in Eretz Yisrael any more, whereas it „once probably“ occurred there „more frequently“. This is incorrect. The tree did not grow in Eretz Yisrael in antiquity either, and pistachios could come into consideration for remote antiquity at most as transit goods, if one wished to assume, against the sources, that the tree already grew in Syria in high antiquity.

Antiquity considered the pistachio a hybrid of the almond tree and the terebinth, which preserves a memory of its late appearance: jKil. [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Kilayim] 1, 27^{a}_{52} לוזים ובוטמין (not, as Aruch [=Aruch, ed. A. Kohut] u. a. [=and others], בוטנין) Ḳazwīnī [=Zakariyyā al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt, ed. Wüstenfeld] 2, 25: حبّة الخضراء [ḥabbat al-khaḍrāʾ] grafted onto لوز [lawz] yields fustuḳ. Thus according to the jer. [=Jerusalem] Talmud, Pf. 69, according to the Greek Geoponica writers, and Kaleb [=Kaleb Afendopulo, appendix to Aderet Elijahu] 17^{a}.
Hebr. [=Hebrew] boṭnīm belongs to aram. [=Aramaic] buṭma, has the same meaning, and was treated under P. Terebinthus (s. [=see] above 192).

In Mishnaic Hebrew the pistachio is called פסתקין pl. [=plural], derived from pers. [=Persian] pišteh (ZDMG. [=Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft] 50, 646), like syr. [=Syriac] ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא]*) [Samar. [=Samaritan (Targum)] ביצטקין Gn. [=Genesis] 43, 11 LA. [=variant reading] ביסטקין] and, borrowed from it, arab. [=Arabic] fustuḳ**).

[p. 200] Ns. [=Neo-Syriac]: also ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא] PSm. [=Payne Smith, Thesaurus syriacus] 3199. 3838. Maclean [=A. J. Maclean, A dictionary of the dialect of vernacular Syriac] sv. [=sub voce]: a nut, probably imprecise for a pistachio nut. From Malula, Bergsträsser [=G. Bergsträsser, Neuaramäische Märchen; Glossar des neuaramäischen Dialekts von Maʿlūla] 93_{19}, Glossar [=G. Bergsträsser, Glossar des neuaramäischen Dialekts von Maʿlūla] 27 records: fuscḳō. A tract of land covered with pistachio trees east of Malūlā: ṣaḥrṯa 85. Foreign-language material: On Gn. 43, 11, Raši [=Rashi, commentary] cites for boṭnīm the explanation of R. [=Rabbi] Machir: פשטציאם ed. [=edition] Berliner [=A. Berliner (ed.), Raschi: Commentar zum Pentateuch], פישטקיאם Bible ed. Basel 1620. Raši states that he does not know what bŏṭnīm are, but that he found the explanation pistazias in R. Machir. This, however, he evidently does not know, and he combines it with the word aparsĕḳīn, peach. Ibn Esra [=Abraham Ibn Ezra, commentary] likewise knows nothing of pistachios. He says that some take boṭnīm to be walnuts. RDK. [=Rabbi David Kimhi, Sefer ha-Shorashim]: pignola, according to others: fustuḳ. פיניוניש Epstein, Miḳadm. [=A. Epstein, Miḳadmonijjōt ha-jĕhūdīm] 126 = boṭnīm. Nocili, avellana: Bacher, Prüfstein d. Men. b. Salomo [=Wilhelm Bacher, Der Prüfstein des Menachem ben Salomo], p. [=page] 3 n. [=note] = boṭnīm. Sechel tōb [=Menahem ben Solomon, Sekhel Tov, ed. S. Buber], p. 11: boṭnīm is the resin of the tree boṭna: the tree = לרזו, the resin = טרגנטו. In Mb. [=?] 31 boṭnīm is rendered by פיטולש (l. [=read] pignolas).
